title: 4 days Upper Lower program review
summary: He reviews a viewer's 4-day upper/lower program aimed at growing muscle via compound progression. He suggests ordering upper before lower, widening the squat rep range to 6-10, superset arm work and add triceps long-head work, doubling shrug sets, and not combining bench press and weighted dips as main lifts on the same day.

claims.claim: Progressing on main compound lifts is a fairly good way to increase overall muscularity.
Weighted pull-ups are a very good home addition to gym training.
Neck curls four times a week is serious neck volume and will bring good neck gains.
Uphill running is tough on hamstrings and glutes, decent even for size though below resistance training, and unmatched for cardio.

Avoiding supinated movements may hurt biceps gains long term, though some claim neutral grip builds biceps as well or better; he grew his with supinated movements, but it's a worthwhile experiment if supination hurts.
In a 4-day upper/lower, put lower second so the second lower day falls right before the weekend: lower days carry more tonnage, lower-back stress and damage, and benefit from the extended rest.
He personally can't start his week with lower body; after his Sunday rest he needs the lighter upper body day to start.

A 4x8-10 squat evolving range is too narrow to progress: after hitting 10s, adding even 5 lbs may not allow 8s, and narrow ranges drift toward sandbagged 5x5-style training. Widen it to 4x6-10; 6-12 starts getting too wide.
3x10-12 on RDLs is fine if heavy: the RDL starts with the negative, so it's easier to grind reps than on squats.
Bulgarian split squats at 3x15-18 are 'fixated tonnage' with a small buffer to ease load jumps; combined with squats it's plenty for quads.
He dislikes putting upper body work (hammer curls, pushdowns, triceps extensions) on lower days because it loses synergy and turns the day into a body part split.
The program lacks triceps long-head work; replace bodyweight triceps extensions with overhead extensions, French presses or skull crushers.
Arm work: superset pushdowns with hammer curls then finish with long-head work; with high-intensity 3-set work, supersets are better than giant sets.
When the same day repeats three days later, a wider evolving rep range gives more control over volume and intensity if recovery is imperfect.
A 3x5-style bench (5x3-4) followed by back-off sets is good; back-offs after a 5x5 would be useless. Three back-off sets is excellent.
Pair low-rep strength sets with a 5-8 rep back-off range: if strength sets come in at 3s, push back-offs toward 8; if at 4s, go heavier on back-offs.
Keep weighted pull-ups in low rep ranges; 3x8 is good as it sandbags a lift where form breakdown is harmful and shifts the target muscles.
An 8-12 evolving range suits the overhead press, which feeds off volume and progresses slowly, making up for only 3 sets.
Two sets of shrugs, even with iso holds, is too little; do four, since traps can take huge punishment.

Bench, back-off bench, overhead press and weighted dips on one day is too many compounds; rotate bench and weighted dips as the strength lift (e.g. 2-month blocks or alternating), keeping back-off bench always.
Between bench and dips, the bench suffers more from breaks; calisthenics movements are ingrained and you lose little technical mastery.
Face pulls at 3x20-25 and cable laterals at 4x10-15 are good rep ranges and can be supersetted without hurting performance.
In upper/lower programs the upper day usually ends up with more tonnage than the lower day, contrary to expectations.
Dumbbell rows and pull-ups complement each other rather than being interchangeable; a vertical and horizontal pull on the same day is good, unlike bench plus dips.
RDLs without deadlifts leave the lower back less developed than it could be; heavy compounds and twice-weekly high-rep overhead pressing train the core plenty.
